method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease' (published 3 July 2019), 21 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC6618900). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review) 'Drug-induced movement disorders' (published 1 April 2019), 9 claims; LICENCE: (c) NPS MedicineWise 2019 (no open licence; the article page states none) (read at NCBI PMC record PMC6478951 <permissions> element; australianprescriber.tg.org.au article page). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every edition 1.0 claim (S1, EHDN task force 2019) unchanged and adds S2, an Australian Prescriber review of drug-induced movement disorders, for the wider PBS condition (tardive and other drug-induced hyperkinetic disorders) and for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which tetrabenazine can cause. No Australian Huntington disease guideline was found (Europe PMC searches 2026-09-24: Huntington with guideline/consensus/recommendation in the title 2019-2026; Huntington with Australia and guideline/consensus/management; Australian Prescriber (ISSN 0312-8008) for Huntington, chorea or tetrabenazine).

claims.claim: **HD is an autosomal-dominant CAG-repeat disorder of the HTT gene; 40 or more repeats are fully penetrant.** It causes motor, cognitive and psychiatric disorders, and death occurs about 20 years after symptoms start.
claims.source_text: with a genetic autosomal-dominant inheritance, that first involves basal ganglia (caudate nucleus and putamen) and results from expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene: alleles with 40 or more repeats are fully penetrant. … Death occurs about 20 years after the onset of symptoms.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stress, fatigue and intercurrent illness (anxiety, digestive, infectious or painful conditions) can worsen any HD symptom;** assess and treat them alongside the HD symptoms.
claims.source_text: Given that any HD symptoms may be worsened by stress, fatigue, and intercurrent disorders (e.g., anxiety, digestive disorders, infectious or painful conditions, etc.), these aspects must be assessed and should be treated with appropriate measures alongside managing the Huntington's symptoms.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Worsening involuntary movements or a change in behaviour should prompt a search for discomfort, especially pain.**
claims.source_text: Behavioral change or worsening of involuntary movements should trigger the search for an underlying source of discomfort, and in particular pain.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat chorea with drugs when it distresses or discomforts the patient.**
claims.source_text: Drug treatment should be considered if chorea causes the patient distress or discomfort.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Tetrabenazine is a first-line treatment for chorea (Grade A), unless depression is poorly controlled or there are suicidal thoughts.**
claims.source_text: Tetrabenazine is one of the first-line treatments for this symptom (Grade A) () unless the patient suffers from not well-managed depression or suicidal thoughts.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A second-generation neuroleptic is first line (Grade B) particularly when personality, behavioural or psychotic disorders accompany the chorea.**
claims.source_text: Second generation neuroleptics (Grade B) (, ) are first-line treatments for this symptom in particular when the patients have associated personality and/or behavioral or psychotic disorders.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use one antichorea drug, not a combination:** combinations raise the risk of adverse effects and complicate management of non-motor symptoms.
claims.source_text: Monotherapy to treat chorea is preferred because combination therapy increases the risk of adverse effects and may complicate the management of non-motor symptoms.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Deutetrabenazine (Grade A) may be an alternative to tetrabenazine where it is authorised**, as in the USA.
claims.source_text: Except for deutetrabenazine (Grade A) (, ), none of the studies justified to modify the recommendations. Deutetrabenazine may indeed be proposed as an alternative to tetrabenazine for the treatment of chorea in countries where the marketing authorization is already obtained, like in the USA.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Tetrabenazine and neuroleptics can cause or worsen rigidity.** If function suffers, consider lowering the dose or stopping, weighing benefit on chorea or behaviour against the rigidity.
claims.source_text: Rigidity may be increased or induced by the use of neuroleptics or tetrabenazine. If this impacts the functional capacity of the patient, a reduction in dosage or the withdrawal of neuroleptics and/or tetrabenazine should be considered considering overall benefit on chorea and/or behavioral symptoms vs. severity of rigidity.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Akathisia: look for a drug cause first.** Tetrabenazine, neuroleptics and SSRIs can cause it; lowering the dose or switching may help.
claims.source_text: An iatrogenic cause of akathisia should be investigated as the priority. Tetrabenazine (Grade C) (, ), neuroleptics and Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) may cause akathisia in HD and reducing the dose or changing the treatment may be helpful.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Antichorea drugs can help or hinder:** they may improve gait and balance, but side effects (sedation, parkinsonism) can impair swallowing and walking, so reassess them regularly.
claims.source_text: Pharmaceutical management of chorea may improve walking and balance as they can be affected by chorea (Grade C) (-). However, they should always be used cautiously and regularly reassessed as their adverse effects may also aggravate walking disorders. … However, side effects of treatments for chorea (e.g., sedation, attention, and parkinsonism) might also negatively impact swallowing capacities.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Akathisia usually eases once the causative drug is stopped.** Clonidine, mirtazapine, amantadine, benzodiazepines, beta blockers and anticholinergics have all been tried, with variable effect and little evidence.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Drug-induced parkinsonism** (from dopamine-blocking drugs) is usually symmetrical and akinetic-rigid, comes on over days to months, responds poorly to levodopa, dopamine agonists and anticholinergics, and normally resolves fully when the drug is stopped.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Tetrabenazine, like antipsychotics, lithium and metoclopramide, can cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome.** Suspect it with dopamine-blocker exposure (or dopamine-agonist withdrawal) in the last 72 hours plus temperature over 38 °C on two or more readings, rigidity, altered mental state, raised creatine kinase and autonomic instability.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome means hospital admission:** stop the causative drugs at once, give supportive care (intensive care if severe) and a dopaminergic drug, usually bromocriptine; benzodiazepines can ease rigidity. It usually settles within 2–3 weeks, so continue bromocriptine for several weeks.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Tardive disorders start during a drug or within weeks of stopping it and persist for at least one month,** after at least three months of exposure (one month in adults over 60). Antipsychotics, the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, and cinnarizine or flunarizine are the usual causes.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Tardive forms include orobuccolingual dyskinesia, stereotypies, akathisia, dystonia, myoclonus, tremor, tics and parkinsonism.** Stopping long-term antipsychotics abruptly can trigger withdrawal dyskinesia, especially in children; it settles when the drug is restarted and then tapered slowly.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **There is no good evidence on how to treat tardive disorders.** The usual approach is to withdraw the causative drug and trial a combination of drugs (clonazepam especially for myoclonus). Sometimes the drug has to be restarted or switched to an atypical antipsychotic, with clozapine preferred in chronic psychosis.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The VMAT2 inhibitors deutetrabenazine and valbenazine are the newest proposed options;** tetrabenazine, amantadine and propranolol have also been tried.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Vitamin B6 and Ginkgo biloba are probably helpful** (vitamin E results conflict), but Ginkgo's antiplatelet effect needs care with antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs. Preventive anticholinergics have no supporting evidence. Botulinum toxin can help focal tardive dystonia, and pallidal deep brain stimulation can work very well in severe cases.
claims.locator: Duma SR, Fung VSC (Movement Disorders Unit, Westmead Hospital, Sydney), Australian Prescriber 42:56-61, doi 10.18773/austprescr.2019.014 (review), 'Drug-induced movement disorders', published 1 April 2019, https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/drug-induced-movement-disorders.html, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Akinetic-rigid symptoms, especially in juvenile HD, may respond partially and temporarily to levodopa (Grade C);** start slowly, and the daily dose is usually lower than in Parkinson disease.
claims.source_text: Levodopa may provide partial and temporary relief of the akinetic-rigid symptoms of HD, especially in juvenile forms (Grade C) (-). Treatment with levodopa should be started gradually and the total daily dose is usually lower than in Parkinson's disease.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Myoclonus affecting function: sodium valproate or clonazepam, alone or together, in escalating doses (Grade C);** levetiracetam is an alternative.
claims.source_text: In case of myoclonus impacting the functional capacity of the patients, treatment with sodium valproate or clonazepam, used alone or in combination, and in escalating doses, is recommended (Grade C) (-). Levetiracetam is a therapeutic alternative for the same indication.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Assess swallowing regularly and refer to a speech and language therapist as soon as problems appear (Grade C).** Discuss gastrostomy (PEG) early, while the patient can still weigh it.
claims.source_text: Regular assessment of swallowing disorders should be provided throughout the progression of the disease (Grade C) () and referral to a Speech and Language Therapist is recommended as soon as the disorders appear (Grade C) … PEG should be anticipated and discussed with relatives and patients still able to understand the benefits and burdens of the methods.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer early to physiotherapy;** exercise programmes help overall function and independence (Grade B).
claims.source_text: Early referral to a physiotherapist is recommended in order to facilitate the development of a therapeutic relationship, promote sustainable exercise behaviors and ensure long-term functional … Physiotherapy and/or personalized exercise programs (Grade B) () are beneficial for the overall functional ability, motor function, and independence in HD
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Assess suicide risk at every stage,** especially at diagnosis and when the disease begins to affect daily life.
claims.source_text: Suicide risk should be assessed in HD irrespective of the stage, being particularly vigilant at the time of diagnosis and when the disease starts to impact on day-to-day life.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Depression (Grade B):** use an SSRI or SNRI, or mianserin or mirtazapine when sleep is disturbed. Consult a psychiatrist for resistant or psychotic depression.
claims.source_text: An antidepressant may be suggested if depression occurs in HD (Grade B) (). It is recommended to use a selective SSRI or a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), or alternatively Mianserin or Mirtazapine, in case of sleep disruption. … In the case of resistant depression, or depression associated with psychotic symptoms, a psychiatrist should be consulted.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Irritability:** SSRIs are first line (Grade C), often near the maximum dose; for aggressive behaviour a neuroleptic is first line (Grade C).
claims.source_text: Whilst SSRIs are first lines for irritability (Grade C) (, ), it may be necessary to use them at or near the maximum recommended dose in order to be effective. … In patients with aggressive behavior, the recommended first-line treatment is a neuroleptic (Grade C)
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hallucinations and delusions:** stop other psychotropic drugs, then use a second-generation neuroleptic (Grade C); clozapine is first line in akinetic HD with disabling parkinsonism.
claims.source_text: The use by the patient of psychotropic agents should be searched for and interrupted in case of hallucinations and delusions. Second generation neuroleptics are the first line treatment for hallucinations and delusions (Grade C) (, -). Clozapine should be proposed as the first-line treatment in the case of akinetic forms of HD with debilitating Parkinsonian symptoms.
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cognitive symptoms: no drug is recommended;** rehabilitation may help for a time (Grade B).
claims.source_text: Based on present knowledge, no pharmacological treatment is recommended for the treatment of cognitive symptoms. Multiple rehabilitation strategies (speech therapy, occupational therapy, cognitive and psychomotricity) might improve or stabilize transitorily cognitive functions at some point of time in the course of the disease (Grade B)
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Weight loss: intervene when unintended loss exceeds 10% over 3–6 months, or 5% over 3–6 months with a BMI below 20 kg/m2.** Use dietitian-supervised high-calorie, high-protein supplements (Grade C).
claims.source_text: medical and/or social intervention is recommended when unintended weight loss is higher than 10% within last 3-6 months or when BMI is <20 kg/m2 and unintentional weight loss of 5% is observed within last 3-6 months. When weight loss is observed, high-calorie and high-protein food supplements should be prescribed under instruction and monitored by a dietician/nutritionist (Grade C)
claims.locator: European Huntington's Disease Network guidelines task force (Bachoud-Lévi AC, Ferreira J, Massart R, et al.), Frontiers in Neurology vol 10, doi 10.3389/fneur.2019.00710, 'International Guidelines for the Treatment of Huntington's Disease', published 3 July 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6618900/, retrieved 2026-09-23
